title: Whole-space squared displacement (Proposition 4.3)
subtitle: G3 · Section 4 · positive squared displacement, Ky Fan dominance, and Q-norms
adaptation: Standalone mathematical companion to the G3 narration. Structured around the exact restricted-displacement, direct-sum, pinching, and Q-norm argument. Figure is an original locally authored SVG.

slides.title: What Proposition 4.3 actually compares
slides.lead: The optimization acts on the entire ambient space, but its objective is the positive square of the displacement.
body: Let U and V be compatible subspaces with a canonical direct rotation D. A competitor W is unitary and carries U onto V. Both move vectors in the ambient Hilbert space, including vectors outside U.

Proposition 4.3 compares the Ky Fan prefixes of the squared displacement operators. It establishes an invariant-norm inequality for those positive operators; the same statement cannot simply be transferred to every norm of the unsquared displacement.
slides.takeaway: The object compared is (I−W)*(I−W), not I−W itself.

slides.title: The positive displacement square
slides.lead: A unitary displacement becomes a positive operator when multiplied by its adjoint.
body: For every vector x, the quadratic form of G_W is ‖x−Wx‖². Its nonnegative eigenvalues are precisely the squared singular values of I−W.
The direct rotation D has an analogous square G_D. Proposition 4.3 controls all Ky Fan prefix sums of the spectra of these two positive operators.
slides.takeaway: Positive displacement energy exposes the singular-value squares.

slides.title: Restricted optimality: the input theorem
slides.lead: The principal angles give a pointwise singular-value lower bound for every restricted competitor.
body: On a principal vector of angle θ, the canonical rotation moves by the chord 2 sin(θ/2). For an arbitrary competitor W, projection onto V gives a lower bound for ‖x−Wx‖.

The span of the k largest-angle principal vectors has projection length at most cos(θ_k) on its unit sphere. Singular-value min–max then gives the kth restricted displacement inequality even if W mixes principal directions.
slides.takeaway: The restricted theorem is a singular-value inequality, not a pointwise Gram-operator comparison.

slides.title: A second restriction: the orthogonal complement
slides.lead: Controlling the source subspace alone does not control the whole ambient displacement.
body: Split the ambient space into U and U⊥. The canonical direct rotation also sends U⊥ onto V⊥ and is the direct rotation for that complementary pair.

Apply the same restricted singular-value comparison to U⊥. Squaring preserves both lists of nonnegative singular values, producing separate Ky Fan comparisons for the two diagonal compressions of the squared displacement.
slides.takeaway: The complement supplies the second half of the whole-space comparison.

slides.title: Ky Fan sums combine the two blocks
slides.lead: The kth Ky Fan sum of a block diagonal positive operator is obtained by merging two sorted eigenvalue lists.
body: Take the sorted eigenvalue lists of the two restrictions. A prefix of the merged list takes i values from one block and k−i from the other, for the maximizing split.
Because the direct rotation is no larger on every restricted prefix, it is no larger after the two lists are merged. This proves a Ky Fan comparison for the diagonal blocks combined.
slides.takeaway: Merging ranked lists preserves the two separate prefix inequalities.

slides.title: Pinching removes a competitor’s cross blocks
slides.lead: A competing transporter can mix U and U⊥, so its displacement square need not be block diagonal.
body: The reflection J equals +1 on U and −1 on U⊥. Averaging G with JGJ cancels off-diagonal blocks while preserving the two diagonal compressions.

Each Ky Fan norm is convex and invariant under unitary conjugation. Consequently the pinched operator has no larger Ky Fan prefixes than G itself. For the direct rotation, G_D is already block diagonal, so pinching leaves it unchanged.
slides.takeaway: The key middle inequality is K_k(P(G_W)) ≤ K_k(G_W).

slides.title: Proposition 4.3: the valid conclusion
slides.lead: Compose restricted optimality, the direct-sum comparison, and pinching.
body: The direct squared displacement is no larger in every Ky Fan prefix. Ky Fan dominance extends this to all unitarily invariant norms applied to the positive squares.
The conclusion concerns sums of the largest eigenvalues. It does not assert that every individual eigenvalue of G_D is smaller than the corresponding eigenvalue of G_W.
slides.takeaway: The whole-space theorem is precisely a weak-majorization statement for squared singular values.

slides.title: A positive pinching example
slides.lead: Pinching can decrease the largest eigenvalue while increasing a smaller eigenvalue.
body: The first matrix is positive, with eigenvalues 5 and 1. The pinched matrix is positive with eigenvalues 3 and 3.
Its largest eigenvalue decreases from 5 to 3 while its smaller eigenvalue increases from 1 to 3. Prefix sums are still controlled: 3 ≤ 5 and 3+3 = 5+1.
slides.takeaway: Weak majorization is weaker than entrywise eigenvalue comparison.

slides.title: Which unsquared norms follow?
slides.lead: A Q-norm squares through a unitarily invariant norm of the positive Gram operator.
body: Operator and Frobenius norms satisfy this property, as do the Schatten p norms with p ≥ 2. The exponent p/2 is then at least 1, so the right-hand side is again a unitarily invariant norm.
Applying the squared-displacement theorem to M proves N(I−D) ≤ N(I−W) for these Q-norms. Extra ideal-membership hypotheses are required for infinite-dimensional finite-gauge claims.
slides.takeaway: The squared theorem gives full-displacement optimality for Q-norms.

slides.title: Why the unsquared trace norm is different
slides.lead: The trace norm adds singular values; the squared theorem adds squares before applying a symmetric gauge.
body: For a direct rotation with four equal displacement singular values a and a competitor with values b,b,0,0, the squared prefixes may favor the direct rotation while 4a exceeds 2b.
Taking square roots can reverse the order of total sums because square root is concave. Therefore the squared-displacement theorem does not establish universal unsquared trace-norm optimality.
slides.takeaway: A valid squared comparison cannot be read as an arbitrary unsquared comparison.

slides.title: Real planar comparison at sixty degrees
slides.lead: Already in one real principal plane, competing orientation types have different displacement lists.
body: Direct rotation minimizes both the operator and squared Frobenius norms in the usual acute planar setting. For trace norm its cost is 4 sin(θ/2), while reflection costs 2.
They tie at θ = 60°. Above that angle the reflection has smaller trace cost. In higher dimensions, mixing between principal planes creates additional competitors even below this planar threshold.
slides.takeaway: The planar threshold does not establish a global higher-dimensional statement.

slides.title: Proof map and exact scope
slides.lead: The whole proof depends on keeping the measured operator and its hypotheses fixed.
body: Prove restricted singular-value optimality on U and U⊥. Square the restricted lists. Merge them by Ky Fan direct-sum comparison. Pinch away the competitor’s cross blocks. Since the direct square is block diagonal, conclude Ky Fan dominance for G_D.

This argument gives every unitarily invariant norm of the positive squared operator and, through Q-norm identities, selected norms of the unsquared displacement. The historical infinite-dimensional statement includes compact-angle and crossed-defect assumptions; the acute finite-dimensional setting avoids those additional existence issues.
slides.takeaway: Proposition 4.3 survives; the broader unsquared assertion needs a separate test.
